lessons.title: Where Equity Comes From in India: Founders, Angels, VCs and PE Funds

children.text: "We are talking to investors." That sentence covers an enormous range. The person writing a ₹25 lakh cheque from their own bank account and the fund writing ₹500 crore from a pool of pension money are both buying equity, but almost nothing else about them is the same. They enter at different stages, expect different returns, hold for different periods and want different things from you.
This lesson maps who actually supplies equity in India, and more usefully, explains why each one behaves the way it does.

body.text: Every equity investor buys the same thing: a share of your company. What differs is whose money they are using, how long they can wait, and how they plan to get out. Those three facts explain almost everything an investor will ask of you.

children.text: The Supplier Map

body.caption: Who supplies equity to Indian companies

cells: Nothing. It is your own money
Belief in you, usually not a rigorous financial case
A large market, a credible founder, an early signal of demand
Early traction and a path to a Series A within 18 months
Fast revenue growth and a business that can become very large
Scale, improving unit economics, a visible listing in a few years
Steady cash flows, often a controlling stake
A commercial fit with their own business, not only a financial return
Direct access to private companies, often through networks

body.title: Indicative cheque size by investor type (₹ crore)

body.text: These are indicative ranges, not rules. Cheque sizes move with the funding cycle: the same fund that wrote ₹150 crore Series A cheques in 2021 may write ₹40 crore cheques in a tighter market. Ask any fund directly what its typical cheque and ownership target are before you pitch.

children.text: Why Fund Structure Explains Fund Behaviour
Most Indian VC and PE investors are not investing their own money. They raise a fund from
limited partners
: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, family offices and wealthy individuals. That fund has a fixed size, a fixed life of roughly ten years, and a promise attached to it.

markDefs.definition: The institutions and individuals whose money a fund invests: pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, family offices and wealthy individuals. Usually shortened to LPs.

children.text: Fixed life.
The fund must return cash to its LPs, typically within ten years. An investment made in year six has to exit faster than one made in year one.
Fees and [[carry]].
Managers typically charge an annual fee of around 2% and keep about 20% of the profits. They make real money only if the fund performs.
The power law.
In venture, most investments return little or nothing. A small number of huge winners carry the entire fund.

That last point is the one founders feel most directly. A venture fund cannot build a good return out of companies that grow steadily and sell for three times the entry price. It needs a few that grow enormously, so it pushes every company in its portfolio to try.

body.latex: \text{Exit value needed} = \frac{\text{Return the fund needs from this deal}}{\text{Fund ownership at exit}}
body.caption: Why a fund's ownership target and its return target are the same conversation

body.title: The number behind the pressure
body.prompt: A venture fund owns 20% of your company at exit and needs ₹600 crore back from this single investment to make its fund work. What must the company be worth at exit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹600 crore divided by 20% is ₹3,000 crore. This is why a fund that likes your business may still pass: not because it will fail, but because it may never get large enough to matter to a fund of that size. A smaller fund would have said yes to the same company.

body.title: What the whole fund has to deliver
body.prompt: A ₹1,000 crore Indian venture fund tells its LPs it is targeting a 3x gross return over the fund's life. How much must it return in total, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹1,000 crore times 3 is ₹3,000 crore. Spread across perhaps 25 to 30 investments, with many returning nothing, a handful have to return very large multiples. That arithmetic, not impatience, is what drives the growth pressure founders feel.

body.label: The power law, illustrated
body.value: Info Edge invested ₹4.7 crore in Zomato in 2010
body.context: That seed cheque bought roughly 18.5% of the company, and Info Edge put in about ₹86 crore in total between 2010 and 2013. By the time Zomato listed in 2021 and in the years after, the holding was worth tens of thousands of crore. One investment like this can carry an entire portfolio, and both investors and founders behave accordingly.

body.title: The SEBI structure behind almost every Indian fund

children.text: Nearly every Indian VC, PE and angel fund is registered with SEBI as an
alternative investment fund
under the AIF Regulations, 2012. There are three categories.

markDefs.definition: A privately pooled investment vehicle registered with SEBI under the AIF Regulations, 2012. Almost every Indian VC, PE and angel fund is registered as one.

cells: Funds investing in start-ups, early-stage ventures, SMEs, infrastructure and social ventures
Venture capital funds, angel funds, SME funds
Funds that are neither Category I nor III and do not use significant leverage
Most private equity funds, real estate funds, private credit funds
Funds using complex or leveraged strategies, including listed securities
Long-short and other hedge fund strategies

children.text: Angel funds are a sub-category within Category I, and their rules changed materially with the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025, notified on 9 September 2025.
Angel funds may now raise money only from
accredited investor
s.

markDefs.definition: An investor certified as meeting income or net worth thresholds set under SEBI's accreditation framework, and therefore allowed to access products with fewer retail protections.

children.text: The earlier minimum commitment of ₹25 lakh per angel investor and the ₹5 crore minimum corpus were removed.
The minimum investment in a single investee company was reduced from ₹25 lakh to ₹10 lakh, and the ceiling per investee company was raised.
If you are raising from an angel fund, confirm the current position with the fund. This area has changed more than once and the details matter for eligibility.
Venture Capital and Private Equity Are Not the Same Business
The two get used interchangeably in conversation. They are almost opposites in how they make money.

columns.label: Venture capital
points: Invests in loss-making, fast-growing companies
Takes minority stakes, typically 10% to 25%
Makes money from a few outsized winners
Expects many investments to fail completely
Founders stay in charge and keep running the company
Exits through later rounds, an IPO or a strategic sale

columns.label: Private equity
points: Invests in profitable, established companies
Often takes control, sometimes 100%
Makes money from operational improvement and leverage
Cannot afford failures, because cheques are large and few
May replace management or install its own CEO and CFO
Exits by selling to another fund, a strategic buyer or through an IPO

children.text: Indian private equity names worth knowing include ChrysCapital, Kedaara Capital, Multiples Alternate Asset Management and the India arms of global firms such as Blackstone, TPG and Advent. On the venture side, Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia Capital India), Accel India, Blume Ventures and Kalaari Capital are among the most active. Which of them is right for a company depends almost entirely on its stage and profitability.

body.title: Whose cheque is this?
body.question: A 22-year-old profitable Coimbatore pump manufacturer earns ₹60 crore of operating profit a year. The promoter is 68, his children are not interested in the business, and he wants to sell 70% and retire while keeping the company independent. Who is the natural buyer?
options: A private equity fund looking at a buyout
body.explanation: This is a classic Indian buyout. The business is profitable and predictable, the cheque is large, and the seller wants to hand over control. Angels and seed funds operate at a fraction of this size, and a VC fund has no interest in a mature, slow-growing manufacturer.

body.title: Why the pressure to grow?
body.question: A founder complains that her VC keeps pushing for faster growth even though the company is close to profitability at its current size. What best explains the fund's behaviour?
options: The fund earns interest on the money and wants it back sooner
The fund needs a few very large outcomes to make its ten-year fund work, and a modest profitable company cannot provide one
SEBI requires AIFs to grow their portfolio companies
The fund wants to dilute the founder further
body.explanation: Venture returns follow a power law. A steady, modestly profitable company is a fine business but it cannot return a fund. The fund is not being unreasonable so much as following the arithmetic of its own structure, which is exactly why founders should check whether a fund's model matches their ambition before taking its money.

body.title: The 2025 change
body.textWithBlank: Following SEBI's September 2025 amendment, an angel fund may raise money only from ___ investors.
body.explanation: Angel funds were moved to an accredited-investor-only model, while the earlier ₹25 lakh minimum commitment and ₹5 crore minimum corpus requirements were removed.

children.text: Strategic Investors: The Fourth Option

Not every equity investor is a fund. A larger company may invest in a smaller one because the two businesses fit together. Reliance, Tata, Info Edge and many Indian corporates hold stakes in smaller companies for exactly this reason.

columns.label: A strategic investor brings
points: Distribution, customers or supply relationships
Industry credibility that opens doors
Patience, because they are not running a ten-year fund
A possible future acquirer of the whole company

columns.label: A strategic investor also brings
points: A potential competitor inside your data room
Terms that may block you from working with their rivals
Slower decisions, because approvals run through a corporate hierarchy
A right of first refusal that can deter other buyers later

body.title: Two term sheets, same amount
body.scenario: You are the CFO of a four-year-old Ahmedabad company selling supply chain software to textile manufacturers. Revenue is ₹18 crore and growing about 60% a year, and the company is close to breaking even. Two term sheets arrive, both for ₹30 crore. One is from a venture fund taking 18% with a board seat and standard investor protections. The other is from a large textile machinery manufacturer taking 18%, offering access to its 400 existing customers, with a clause giving it the right to match any future offer to buy the company.
body.prompt: How would you compare the two, and what would you want answered before recommending either?
body.modelAnswer:
What is genuinely different here is not the money, it is what comes attached.

The venture fund: brings capital, governance discipline, hiring networks and experience of the next two rounds. It will push hard for growth because its own fund arithmetic demands it. Ask about fund vintage (a fund in year seven needs a faster exit than one in year two), its typical follow-on behaviour, and which portfolio founders you can speak to.

The strategic investor: the 400 customers could be worth more than the ₹30 crore itself, and it may become the eventual acquirer. But look hard at the right-to-match clause. It can deter other bidders from spending time and money on a process they might lose at the last step, which tends to suppress the eventual price. Ask whether competitors of the investor will still buy your software once it is on your cap table, how information flows to the investor, and whether the customer access is contractually committed or merely promised in the pitch.

What I would want before recommending either:
1. A written commitment converting the customer access into specific, measurable terms, otherwise treat it as worth zero.
2. The right-to-match clause narrowed or removed, or at least time-limited.
3. Clarity on who leads the next round: a strategic investor on the cap table can make some financial investors hesitant.
4. The company's own answer to the growth question. If the founders want a steady profitable business, the venture fund is a poor match regardless of terms.

body.title: Questions to ask any equity investor before taking their money
steps: Whose money are you investing, and how old is the fund?
What is your typical cheque size and target ownership?
How many companies at our stage have you backed, and can we speak to three founders?
Do you follow on in later rounds, and what makes you decide not to?
What does a good outcome look like to you for a company like ours?
What do you expect from us in board meetings and monthly reporting?
If we choose to grow steadily rather than aggressively, does that break your model?

body.label: Indian Angel Network
body.description: One of India's oldest angel networks. Useful for seeing how an organised angel group describes its process, cheque sizes and what it screens for before you approach any network.

cards.definition: An individual investing their own money at the earliest stages, typically ₹10 lakh to ₹2 crore.
A SEBI-registered Category I AIF pooling angel money. Since September 2025, open only to accredited investors.
Minority investment in loss-making, fast-growing companies, funded by LPs through a ten-year fund.
Large investment in profitable companies, often buying control and improving operations.
The institutions and individuals whose money a fund invests.
The roughly 20% share of fund profits kept by the managers after returning capital to LPs.
The pattern where a few huge winners produce almost all of a venture fund's returns.
A company, not a fund, investing for commercial fit as well as financial return.

points: Equity in India comes from a ladder of suppliers: founders, friends and family, angels, seed funds, VCs, growth funds, PE funds and strategic investors.
Most funds invest other people's money through a ten-year vehicle, which is why exit timing and ownership targets dominate their thinking.
Venture returns follow a power law, so a VC needs outcomes large enough to return its whole fund.
Venture capital buys minority stakes in loss-making growth companies. Private equity buys control of profitable ones.
Angel funds are Category I AIFs, and SEBI's September 2025 amendment restricted them to accredited investors while removing the old minimum commitment and corpus rules.
A strategic investor can bring customers and credibility, but read the clauses that could limit your future options.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Cheque sizes and return targets are indicative and vary widely by fund and market cycle. Named funds and companies are mentioned as examples of the Indian market, not as recommendations. SEBI rules cited were current as notified in September 2025, and regulations change, so verify before acting.
